result: Time-resolved X-ray diffraction of isolated mouse EDL muscles at 28°C was used to characterize structural changes in thick filaments during muscle contraction. The experimental temperature preserves the thick filament 'off' state and allows reproducible contractions suitable for signal averaging, with calcium dynamics and force production well-characterized at this temperature.
evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C21-C24 establish the experimental approach and justify the choice of 28°C as the experimental temperature. The cited literature (C22-C24) supports that calcium dynamics are characterized and thick filament structure is preserved at this temperature, providing a sound experimental foundation.

result: Sarcomere length measurements using ultra-low-angle X-ray diffraction revealed that sarcomeres shortened by ~12% during tetanus (from 2.4 to 2.13 µm) and remained isometric for ~20 ms after the last stimulus while force declined to 80% of plateau. Mouse EDL exhibits clear isometric and chaotic relaxation phases similar to amphibian muscle.
evaluation: Claims C25-C31 describe sarcomere length changes measured by X-ray diffraction with quantitative precision. The observation of isometric and chaotic relaxation phases (C29-C30) is well-supported by the data and comparison to previous work on amphibian muscle. The 12% sarcomere shortening (C28) is directly calculated from measured lengths.

result: Equatorial X-ray reflections show that myosin motors move radially toward thin filaments before strong actin binding or force generation. The intensity ratio I1,1/I1,0 increased from ~0.4 at rest to ~1.8 at tetanus plateau and ~0.9 at twitch peak, with kinetics faster than force development.
evaluation: Claims C32-C37 describe equatorial reflection changes with quantitative measurements (C34-C35) and temporal relationships (C36). The inference that motors move toward thin filaments before strong binding (C37) is supported by comparison to cited work showing that strong attachment has the same time course as force (Brunello et al., 2006).

result: The first actin layer line (IAL1) increased threefold during tetanus with kinetics similar to force, while the first myosin layer line (IML1) decreased much faster than force development. IML1 decreased similarly in twitch and tetanus but did not recover during isometric relaxation and recovered incompletely during chaotic relaxation.
evaluation: Claims C38-C44 describe layer line intensity changes with clear temporal relationships. The faster decrease of IML1 compared to force (C40-C41) and its incomplete recovery (C43-C44) are directly observed in the data. The inference that loss of helical conformation precedes actin attachment (C41) follows logically from the temporal data.

result: The M6 reflection spacing (SM6) increased by 1.54% during tetanus and 0.95% during twitch, signaling thick filament activation. SM6 increased faster than force at tetanus onset, recovered with force during isometric relaxation, but remained incompletely recovered >120 ms after the last stimulus.
evaluation: Claims C45-C51 describe M6 reflection changes with precise quantitative measurements (C46-C47) and temporal relationships (C49-C51). The association with thick filament activation (C48) is supported by citation to Haselgrove, 1975. The incomplete recovery (C51) is directly observed.

result: The M3 reflection intensity (IM3) showed biphasic behavior during tetanus (initial decrease then threefold increase) but only decreased during twitch. M3 spacing (SM3) increased by 1.36% in tetanus and 0.57% in twitch, faster than force but slower than SM6. SM3 remained constant during isometric relaxation while IM3 recovered, indicating motor disorder.
evaluation: Claims C52-C62 describe complex M3 reflection changes with quantitative measurements (C57-C58) and temporal relationships (C59). The inference that motors become disordered during isometric relaxation (C61) is logically derived from the different behaviors of SM3 and IM3 (C60). The biphasic IM3 response (C53-C55) is interpreted with citation support.

result: A transient 'star' peak appeared in the M3 reflection ~10 ms after stimulation onset with spacing of 14.832 nm during tetanus rise and 14.878 nm at twitch peak. A similar peak was previously observed upon cooling of resting muscle.
evaluation: Claims C63-C66 describe a novel observation with precise spacing measurements (C64-C65). The comparison to previous cooling experiments (C66) provides context, though the mechanistic interpretation remains incomplete. The observation itself is well-documented.

result: Modeling the M3 reflection axial profile showed that at rest nearly all 49 motor layers were ordered (nm=2, nd=46), while at tetanus plateau all layers were ordered (nm=1, nd=49). At twitch peak, only a central region was ordered (nm=9, nd=43). The motor center of mass moved 11 nm from rest to tetanus plateau, with no significant motion during early activation despite loss of helical order.
evaluation: Claims C67-C74 describe modeling results with specific parameter values (C68-C70) and calculated motor movements (C71). The key inference that helical order is lost before motor unfolding (C73) is strongly supported by the observation that IML1 decreased 50% while hbz showed no change during early activation (C72). The 11 nm movement (C71) matches previous work on amphibian muscle.

result: During tetanus activation, structural changes occur in sequence with distinct kinetics: loss of helical order and backbone elongation are fastest (t1/2 ~8 ms), followed by motor radial motion and spacing changes (t1/2 ~11 ms), then actin attachment (t1/2 ~15 ms). This sequence is similar to amphibian muscle but ~3× faster.
evaluation: Claims C75-C85 synthesize the temporal relationships between structural changes with quantitative half-times from Table 2 (C78-C84). The sequential nature of activation (C81-C82) is well-supported by the data. Comparison to amphibian muscle (C85) is appropriately cited. The framework of five phases (C75) provides clear organization.

result: Thick filament activation (t1/2 ~8 ms) is slower than thin filament activation (Ca2+ peak at 2 ms, troponin binding <1 ms, tropomyosin movement t1/2 <4 ms in amphibian muscle) but faster than actin attachment. This establishes thick filament activation as an intermediate regulatory step.
evaluation: Claims C86-C91 establish the temporal hierarchy of activation steps by comparing thick filament kinetics to cited literature on thin filament activation (C87-C89). The conclusion that thick filament activation has two components intermediate between thin filament activation and actin attachment (C90) is well-supported. The mechanistic interpretation (C91) is appropriately cited.

result: At tetanus plateau, thin filaments are fully activated and ~30% of motors are strongly attached to actin. The 11 nm motor center of mass movement matches that in amphibian muscle, suggesting conserved motor conformations across species.
evaluation: Claims C92-C94 describe the tetanus plateau state with appropriate citations for the fraction of attached motors (C92) and comparison to amphibian muscle (C93). The inference about conservation across species (C94) is reasonable given the structural similarities noted.

result: During isometric relaxation, sarcomeres remain isometric for ~20 ms while force decays to 80% of plateau. Motors detach from actin (signaled by decreasing I1,1/I1,0 and IAL1) but thick filament structure does not recover (IML1, SM3 constant), indicating a transient population of disordered motors.
evaluation: Claims C95-C103 describe isometric relaxation with clear evidence from multiple X-ray signals (C99-C102). The inference about disordered motors (C103) logically follows from the delay between motor detachment and structural recovery. Comparison to previous work (C95-C97) is appropriately cited.

result: Motor detachment during relaxation has t1/2 ~23 ms (from AAL1) while helical order recovery has t1/2 ~42 ms (from AML1). At mechanical relaxation, motors had folded back (M3 profile recovered) but only ~80% regained helical packing (IML1 incomplete recovery). This incomplete recovery likely underlies post-tetanic potentiation.
evaluation: Claims C104-C111 describe relaxation kinetics with quantitative half-times and the key observation of incomplete helical recovery despite complete motor folding (C108-C109). The link to post-tetanic potentiation (C110-C111) is well-reasoned and cited. The mechanistic explanation (C111) follows logically.

result: Twitch peak force is ~25% of tetanus plateau force, primarily due to fewer actin-attached motors. Despite likely full troponin calcium occupancy (peak [Ca2+] similar in twitch and tetanus), thick filaments are incompletely activated with significant motors remaining folded, limiting force generation.
evaluation: Claims C112-C118 establish the mechanism of low twitch force through multiple lines of evidence: quantitative force comparison (C112), X-ray evidence of fewer attached motors (C113), calcium data (C114-C115), and incomplete thick filament activation (C116-C117). The causal inference (C118) is well-supported.

result: Twitch duration is primarily determined by thin filament inactivation (Ca2+ transient t1/2 ~2 ms, troponin dissociation t1/2 ~25 ms at 28°C). Thick filament inactivation (IML1 t1/2 ~29 ms) is nearly synchronous with thin filament inactivation and force relaxation, contrasting with delayed thick filament inactivation after tetanus.
evaluation: Claims C119-C123 establish the determinants of twitch duration through comparison of kinetics. The calcium data (C120-C121) combines cited literature with temperature extrapolation. The key finding of synchronous thick and thin filament inactivation in twitch (C123) contrasts clearly with tetanus behavior.

result: The twitch response is limited by incomplete thick filament activation despite transient complete thin filament activation. Motor attachment rate is partly limited by thick filament activation. This dual-filament regulatory framework extends previous thin filament-focused models.
evaluation: Claims C124-C127 synthesize the major findings about twitch regulation. The conclusions about incomplete thick filament activation limiting force (C124) and attachment rate (C125) are well-supported by the data. The significance statement (C127) appropriately frames the contribution.

result: Physiological force generation in the twitch is limited by incomplete thick filament activation and rapid inactivation of both filaments. After tetanus, incomplete reformation of the helical array provides a structural basis for post-tetanic potentiation.
evaluation: Claims C3-C5 summarize major findings from the abstract. These are well-supported by the detailed results on twitch force limitation (C112-C126) and incomplete helical recovery after tetanus (C106-C111). The link to post-tetanic potentiation (C5) is mechanistically explained.
